Xremove ads

Why a third Lenovo Googlebook is compelling

Seeing Lenovo active on three separate SoC tracks shows just how aggressively they are committing to the Googlebook era. While ‘Ruby’ gives us Intel-based Googlebooks and ‘Sapphire’ provides a detachable tablet with MediaTek silicon inside, we’ve not yet seen them partner with Qualcomm to deliver a Snapdragon-powered device yet.

By leveraging Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X platform, a ‘Meru’-based device would deliver the same distinct advantages we see in the other OEM devices using this internal structure:

  • All-day battery efficiency: Taking advantage of ARM architecture to provide fanless or near-silent operation with multi-day standby time.
  • Dedicated NPU performance: Utilizing Qualcomm’s 45+ TOPS NPU to handle local Gemini AI tasks and screen reasoning without hitting system lag.
  • Ultra-thin mobility: Fitting into Lenovo’s popular Yoga or IdeaPad Slim chassis designs for road warriors and students.

The Googlebook launch fleet is growing fast

When Google first pulled back the curtain on Googlebook at The Android Show back in May, they named five core manufacturing partners: Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. At the time, I assumed we might see one primary device from each brand for the launch and near future that will follow.

Xremove ads

Instead, the Chromium Gerrit shows that partners are building multiple form factors across Intel, Qualcomm, and MediaTek silicon. With the assumptions made here, Lenovo alone now appears to have three distinct SoCs now included in their Googlebook portfolio.

One final caveat I’ll throw in: ‘Meru’ is baselined off of ‘Quartz’ to start off with. Though the developer behind this initial effort is clearly tied heavily to Lenovo, ‘Quartz’ is already known as the HP Googlebook 14c, so there’s a small chance that HP is involved here instead. And until more ‘Meru’ commits come in, we won’t know that for sure.

Either way, I’ll be keeping a close eye on the Gerrit as development continues for ‘Meru’, so stay tuned to Chrome Unboxed for more updates as we continue covering what we’re starting to internally call “Googlebook Silly Season”.

item.title: How Google blocked 7 billion abusive notifications a day to clean up Chrome
item.itunes:title: How Google blocked 7 billion abusive notifications a day to clean up Chrome
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

Push notifications on the web started with great intentions: letting web apps send you timely, useful updates without needing a dedicated native application. But over the years, bad actors turned that privilege into a chaotic mess of fake virus warnings, deceptive spam prompts, and relentless pop-ups. They are the worst.

To fix this, the Chrome Security team partnered with Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) and Safe Browsing on a multi-year initiative to eliminate notification abuse. According to a new technical breakdown from Google Security, those layered protections successfully blocked over 7 billion unwanted notifications every single day on Android in Q1 alone.

Xremove ads

Here is a look at how Google is using a defense-in-depth model to eliminate spam notifications, reduce background battery drain, and keep your browsing clutter-free.

The “Swiss cheese” model of defense

Rather than trying to build a single filter to catch every rogue notification, Google implemented what it calls a “Swiss cheese” model: multiple overlapping layers of defense where each layer catches what might slip through another.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

This approach addresses the entire notification lifecycle, from the moment a site asks for permission to server-side message dispatching:

  • Automatic Permission Revocation: Chrome automatically strips notification permissions from sites you haven’t engaged with recently, as well as sites flagged with repeated suspicious notification warnings. These revoked permissions are accessible in Safety Hub if you ever want to restore them.
  • Network-Level Abuse Detection: Malicious actors frequently spin up coordinated networks of domains to bypass single-site blocks. By analyzing service worker activity and behavioral patterns, Chrome identifies and proactively revokes permissions across entire scam and malware networks.
  • Server-Side FCM Throttling: On the server side, Firebase Cloud Messaging now enforces strict message rate limits for the Push API based on domain engagement, permission prompt frequency, and dwell time. Disruptive domains exceeding these thresholds get hit with HTTP 429 errors and are capped at 1,000 messages per minute.
  • Streamlined Permission UI: Updated prompt designs on mobile give users clear, friction-free control to decline prompts without interrupting their browsing, backed by the recent one-tap unsubscribe feature in notification shades.

Less spam, better battery life, and peace of mind

Beyond shielding users from malicious phishing links and fake virus warnings, these behind-the-scenes systems solve a massive quality-of-life issue. Constant background notification checks and rogue push messages drain device battery and clutter notification panels.

By clamping down on abusive traffic before it ever hits your device, Chrome operates noticeably quieter and cleaner.

Xremove ads

How to check and manage your notification permissions

While Chrome’s automated protections handle the heavy lifting in the background, you can always audit your active site permissions manually:

  • On Desktop / ChromeOS: Head to Settings > Privacy and security > Site Settings > Notifications (or type chrome://settings/content/notifications directly into the omnibox).
  • On Android: Tap the three-dot menu (⋮) > Settings > Notifications.

From there, you can review which sites have permission to send alerts, remove unused sites, or set your default preference to silent prompt requests.

item.title: Clarifying Google’s three-tier strategy for the Googlebook era
item.itunes:title: Clarifying Google’s three-tier strategy for the Googlebook era
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

When Google launched the original Chromebook over a decade ago, it started from the bottom up. Early hardware was cheap, plastic, and low-powered, cementing an entry-level reputation that even years of Chromebook Plus and premium flagship efforts couldn’t fix.

With Googlebook, Google is executing the exact opposite playbook. Every leak ahead of this fall’s launch, from the sub-1kg ASUS CX9406 with up to 64GB of RAM to the Snapdragon X Elite Dell XPS 13 all sit firmly in premium territory.

Xremove ads

While those higher-end flagship devices grab the early headlines, a new computing platform cannot survive on one portion of the market alone. Looking across Google’s official roadmap documentation, recent regulatory filings, and our the most recent discovery of Snapdragon X Plus ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ boards, a clear three-tier hardware strategy is officially coming into focus.

The three hardware tiers defined by Google

The three-tier framework isn’t industry speculation; it comes directly from Google’s internal product management hiring documents for the Aluminium OS platform early on in the formation of Googlebook. Google officially defined its target device portfolio across three distinct market segments in the job listing:

Xremove ads

Define the portfolio strategy for consumer and enterprise Android PC hardware, curating a portfolio of devices across various tiers (Chromebook, Chromebook Plus, AL Entry, AL Mass Premium, and AL Premium) that meets the needs of users and the business.

– Google job listing for Senior Product Manager, Android, Laptop and Tablets

We recently saw this naming convention surface in the real world when an upcoming HP Googlebook 14c (TPN-H111, codenamed ‘Quartz’) appeared in the Bluetooth SIG certification database registered officially as the “HP 14 inch Aluminium Premium Book.” Here is how those three tiers break down across the ecosystem from what we can tell thus far:

  1. AL Premium: The halo launch tier arrives this fall and features high-end materials, OLED panels, top-tier silicon (Intel Panther Lake Core Ultra 7, Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite / Snapdragon X2, MediaTek Dimensity CX), and strict hardware requirements across the board.
  2. AL Mass Premium: The high-volume consumer and business sweet spot that should balance 8-core silicon (like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Plus and Intel Core Ultra 5), full 45 TOPS NPU execution, all-day battery efficiency, and a more mid-range pricing structure.
  3. AL Entry: The eventual mainstream and education tier with cost-optimized silicon designed to bring native Android desktop apps and core Gemini capabilities to affordable laptops over time.

Why Google is starting at the top

According to what VP John Maletis shared during our exclusive interview with him, launching top-down with the AL Premium tier is a deliberate, necessary move. To convince developers to build responsive, keyboard-and-mouse-optimized desktop interfaces for heavy apps like Adobe Premiere Pro and Canva, Google had to prove that Googlebook is a legitimate workstation platform capable of competing with Apple’s M-series MacBooks and Windows Copilot+ PCs.

By packing first-wave machines with 32GB to 64GB of RAM, high-resolution OLED displays, and dedicated AI coprocessors, Google establishes high expectations for performance and hardware quality on day one.

Xremove ads

‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ prove the AL Mass Premium tier is already underway

While the fall launch spotlight will belong to flagship models, the AL Mass Premium tier is where Googlebook will capture even more of the mainstream market share.

Our recent look at the Snapdragon X Plus ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ development boards in the Chromium Gerrit is our first concrete proof of this middle tier in action. Because Qualcomm kept the exact same 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU inside the 8-core Snapdragon X Plus as its 12-core Elite sibling, buyers in the midrange bracket will get the exact same instant local AI responsiveness – including screen reasoning, Magic Pointer cursor context, and background task automation – without paying the higher, flagship prices

What the AL Entry tier means for the future of Chromebooks

The presence of an AL Entry tier in Google’s planning documents answers the biggest question looming over the hardware landscape: what happens to affordable Chromebooks for consumers and education?

Xremove ads

While traditional ChromeOS will continue to anchor budget classrooms and entry-level computing for the immediate future, the AL Entry tier confirms that Google envisions a future where Aluminium OS eventually scales across the entire pricing spectrum. Getting to the point where we have enough internal hardware to run the Googlebook OS properly will likely take a bit of time, but the plans are in place already to move in that direction.

A mature platform rollout from day one

Watching Google structure Googlebook into high-end, mid-range and affordable tiers demonstrates how much the company has learned from the past decade of laptop hardware. Rather than scrambling to add premium features to a budget operating system, Google is building a flagship-first ecosystem with a clear, calculated roadmap for mainstream affordability. And I have a sneaking suspicion it is going to work.

When Google launched the original Chromebook over a decade ago, it started from the bottom up. Early hardware was cheap, plastic, and low-powered, cementing an entry-level reputation that even years of Chromebook Plus and premium flagship efforts couldn’t fix.

With Googlebook, Google is executing the exact opposite playbook. Every leak ahead of this fall’s launch, from the sub-1kg ASUS CX9406 with up to 64GB of RAM to the Snapdragon X Elite Dell XPS 13 all sit firmly in premium territory.

Xremove ads

While those higher-end flagship devices grab the early headlines, a new computing platform cannot survive on one portion of the market alone. Looking across Google’s official roadmap documentation, recent regulatory filings, and our the most recent discovery of Snapdragon X Plus ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ boards, a clear three-tier hardware strategy is officially coming into focus.

The three hardware tiers defined by Google

The three-tier framework isn’t industry speculation; it comes directly from Google’s internal product management hiring documents for the Aluminium OS platform early on in the formation of Googlebook. Google officially defined its target device portfolio across three distinct market segments in the job listing:

Xremove ads

Define the portfolio strategy for consumer and enterprise Android PC hardware, curating a portfolio of devices across various tiers (Chromebook, Chromebook Plus, AL Entry, AL Mass Premium, and AL Premium) that meets the needs of users and the business.

– Google job listing for Senior Product Manager, Android, Laptop and Tablets

We recently saw this naming convention surface in the real world when an upcoming HP Googlebook 14c (TPN-H111, codenamed ‘Quartz’) appeared in the Bluetooth SIG certification database registered officially as the “HP 14 inch Aluminium Premium Book.” Here is how those three tiers break down across the ecosystem from what we can tell thus far:

  1. AL Premium: The halo launch tier arrives this fall and features high-end materials, OLED panels, top-tier silicon (Intel Panther Lake Core Ultra 7, Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite / Snapdragon X2, MediaTek Dimensity CX), and strict hardware requirements across the board.
  2. AL Mass Premium: The high-volume consumer and business sweet spot that should balance 8-core silicon (like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Plus and Intel Core Ultra 5), full 45 TOPS NPU execution, all-day battery efficiency, and a more mid-range pricing structure.
  3. AL Entry: The eventual mainstream and education tier with cost-optimized silicon designed to bring native Android desktop apps and core Gemini capabilities to affordable laptops over time.

Why Google is starting at the top

According to what VP John Maletis shared during our exclusive interview with him, launching top-down with the AL Premium tier is a deliberate, necessary move. To convince developers to build responsive, keyboard-and-mouse-optimized desktop interfaces for heavy apps like Adobe Premiere Pro and Canva, Google had to prove that Googlebook is a legitimate workstation platform capable of competing with Apple’s M-series MacBooks and Windows Copilot+ PCs.

By packing first-wave machines with 32GB to 64GB of RAM, high-resolution OLED displays, and dedicated AI coprocessors, Google establishes high expectations for performance and hardware quality on day one.

Xremove ads

‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ prove the AL Mass Premium tier is already underway

While the fall launch spotlight will belong to flagship models, the AL Mass Premium tier is where Googlebook will capture even more of the mainstream market share.

Our recent look at the Snapdragon X Plus ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ development boards in the Chromium Gerrit is our first concrete proof of this middle tier in action. Because Qualcomm kept the exact same 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU inside the 8-core Snapdragon X Plus as its 12-core Elite sibling, buyers in the midrange bracket will get the exact same instant local AI responsiveness – including screen reasoning, Magic Pointer cursor context, and background task automation – without paying the higher, flagship prices

What the AL Entry tier means for the future of Chromebooks

The presence of an AL Entry tier in Google’s planning documents answers the biggest question looming over the hardware landscape: what happens to affordable Chromebooks for consumers and education?

Xremove ads

While traditional ChromeOS will continue to anchor budget classrooms and entry-level computing for the immediate future, the AL Entry tier confirms that Google envisions a future where Aluminium OS eventually scales across the entire pricing spectrum. Getting to the point where we have enough internal hardware to run the Googlebook OS properly will likely take a bit of time, but the plans are in place already to move in that direction.

A mature platform rollout from day one

Watching Google structure Googlebook into high-end, mid-range and affordable tiers demonstrates how much the company has learned from the past decade of laptop hardware. Rather than scrambling to add premium features to a budget operating system, Google is building a flagship-first ecosystem with a clear, calculated roadmap for mainstream affordability. And I have a sneaking suspicion it is going to work.

item.itunes:title: Dell’s more-affordable Snapdragon X Plus Googlebook lineup comes into focus
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:

Over the last few weeks, the initial Googlebook leaks have centered heavily on what will likely turn out being higher-end, more expensive hardware. From Intel Panther Lake in the ASUS CX9406 and Acer Googlebook 14 to 12-core Snapdragon X Elite chips in the HP Googlebook 14c and Dell XPS 13, there’s no question that early comments from our conversation with Google VP John Maletis about the level of launch hardware for Googlebook were spot on.

While those premium machines make for great headlines and make us here at Chrome Unboxed quite excited, Google’s new desktop ecosystem will eventually need to reach outside the high-end bracket to capture more mainstream buyers. Thanks to some fresh new finds in the Chromium Gerrit, we now have our first look at how part of that broader device strategy will play out.

Xremove ads

Two new development boards codenamed ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ have surfaced, revealing that Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Plus is officially joining the Googlebook family, and the underlying code points to an expanded lineup from Dell.

The ‘Bluey’ family splits into Elite and Plus tiers

According to code analysis from GbookHub, Qualcomm’s primary Googlebook reference platform, codenamed ‘Bluey’, has officially branched into two distinct hardware tracks:

Featured Videos

Xremove ads
  • ‘BlueyH’ (Premium Tier): Configured around Qualcomm’s “Hamoa” architecture, which powers the 12-core Snapdragon X Elite (X1E-80-100) found in HP’s Googlebook 14c and Dell’s XPS Googlebook.
  • ‘Bluey’ (Mass Premium Tier): Configured specifically for the 8-core Snapdragon X Plus (X1P-42-100), serving as the foundation for ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’.

Seeing explicit board configs added for the X1P-42-100 proves that Google and Qualcomm are actively engineering machines designed to hit a likely sweet-spot of $599 to $799 rather than restricting the platform to higher-end, more expensive hardware.

What Gerrit commits tell us about Dell’s plans

What makes ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ especially interesting is their relationship to other devices we’ve been tracking. In the Chromium Gerrit, both of these new boards were constructed by directly cloning the repository of Dell’s ‘Mica’ baseboard (the board behind the upcoming Snapdragon-powered Dell XPS 13 Googlebook).

While they share the same architectural roots as ‘Mica’, developers have made specific hardware modifications in the firmware:

Xremove ads
  • Adjusted clock speeds: The motherboard base clock has been reduced from 100 MHz down to 75 MHz to match the power envelope of the Snapdragon X Plus.
  • Retained XPS-style chassis traits: Both boards carry over key ‘Mica’ hardware descriptors, including an integrated fingerprint sensor and an all-USB-C port layout with no legacy USB-A ports.
  • 8-core Oryon CPU cluster: Delivering snappy day-to-day multitasking and exceptional battery efficiency without the thermal demands of a 12-core die.

Dell’s multi-device strategy: XPS 13 at the top, Inspiron in the middle?

Seeing Dell’s baseboard blueprint spawn two distinct Snapdragon X Plus derivatives suggests Dell isn’t just dipping a single toe into the Googlebook waters with a single XPS model.

Instead, Dell appears to be building a cohesive family of ARM-powered Googlebooks. While ‘Mica’ anchors the ultra-premium tier with a 12-core Snapdragon X Elite and an OLED panel, ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ look like the foundation for more affordable companion devices: potentially reviving familiar Dell consumer branding like Inspiron or Latitude for the Googlebook era.

Full 45 TOPS NPU power without the flagship price tag

The best part about seeing the Snapdragon X Plus enter the Googlebook lineup is that users won’t have to sacrifice on-device AI capabilities to save money.

Xremove ads

Qualcomm kept the exact same 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU inside the Snapdragon X Plus as its top-tier Elite sibling. That means ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ will handle local Gemini features like screen reasoning, Magic Pointer cursor context, and real-time audio transcription with the exact same speed and responsiveness as a $1000+ flagship.

A complete hardware ecosystem is coming into focus

When Google announced Googlebook back in May, the big question was whether we’d see a healthy range of hardware choices or just a handful of expensive showcase laptops.

Watching Dell expand its Gerrit footprint from the flagship ‘Mica’ to the Snapdragon X Plus-powered ‘Annite’ and ‘Pic’ shows that OEM partners are planning for serious volume across multiple price points. We’ll continue tracking these boards closely as firmware locks approach, so stay tuned for more updates!

Xremove ads

item.title: The Pixel Watch 5 is here, and its GPS upgrades could be a huge win for runners
item.itunes:title: The Pixel Watch 5 is here, and its GPS upgrades could be a huge win for runners
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

Google just took the wraps off the Pixel Watch 5 yesterday at their annual hardware event in NYC, and rather than completely reinventing the wheel, it looks like a solid, calculated refinement of last year’s model. The new watch leans heavily into proactive Gemini intelligence and introduces a fresh batch of health tracking features.

But as someone who has tested every single Pixel Watch and many other wearables over the years, I know the specs on paper are only half the story. It is how these features actually hold up in a daily workflow that matters, and there is one specific upgrade here that really has my attention.

Xremove ads

Pixel Watch 5 GPS accuracy could be a game-changer

As a runner, I am incredibly eager to test the improved GPS tracking on the new Pixel Watch 5. Google is making some remarkably bold claims here, stating that this watch delivers “2X greater accuracy in the toughest environments” and explicitly claiming it outperforms heavy-hitters like the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro.

To pull this off, Google says they are leveraging the advanced technology behind Google Maps to trace satellite ray paths through 3D building models, while also tapping into a global network of weather reference stations to adjust readings for local atmospheric conditions in real-time. Google already has a massive, highly detailed database of the entire world thanks to Google Earth and Maps, so it makes sense that they would be the ones who could use things like ‘signal fusion’ and 3D modeling to solve this problem.

Xremove ads
Pre-order the Pixel Watch 5 at Best buy

Early testing from expert sports watch reviewer DC Rainmaker—who flew to the dense urban canyons of New York City specifically to test this claim—seems to back this up, noting that Google’s GPS accuracy improvements are “incredibly impressive.” If they can pull off this level of accuracy in a standard, everyday smartwatch rather than a bulky “Ultra” model, this could be a huge win for Google, honestly.

Gemini Intelligence and hardware upgrades

And all of this new tracking and AI processing is driven by a few notable hardware improvements under the hood. The Pixel Watch 5 is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, packing 50% more RAM and a 12% CPU boost over the previous generation, making it 20% faster overall.

That extra headroom is largely dedicated to Gemini. Google has introduced “Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions,” which turns complex, multi-step tasks into seamless one-tap actions on your wrist. If someone asks you when a family dinner is, Gemini can automatically pull the info from your calendar and surface it without you having to dig through your phone. You can even interact with it using new double-pinch gestures, and the popular “Raise to Talk” feature now processes core actions instantly with low latency, even when offline.

Xremove ads

Google says the 41mm model will net you up to 30 hours of battery life, while the larger 45mm model can push up to 40 hours with the always-on display.

New Health Guardian features look very interesting

On the health front, Google is also introducing “Health Guardian” features designed to catch subtle shifts in your wellness before they become emergencies. A notable addition is breathing emergency detection. By monitoring your blood oxygen saturation using a combination of sensors and on-device AI, the watch can detect severe drops caused by things like choking or severe pneumonia, and automatically call emergency services if you are unresponsive (launching first in Europe).

The Pixel Watch 5 will also start generating monthly trend summaries for things like blood pressure, sleep breathing quality, and insulin resistance based on your sensor data. For anyone trying to keep a closer eye on their metabolic and cardiovascular health, getting a readable summary directly from your wrist is incredibly practical. It is worth noting that most of these particular features are app-based and will be coming to other Pixel watches later this fall.

Xremove ads

Lastly, it’s worth pointing out that these new features do come with a slight price bump. The Pixel Watch 5 is available for pre-order right now and will hit shelves on August 20. The 41mm model starts at $399, while the 45mm model comes in at $429. There is also a slick $579 Stephen Curry Special Edition in the 45mm size that features an exclusive sweat-wicking performance loop band, arriving a bit later on September 3.

Yes, this is the year of refinement for Google, but overall, I think the Pixel Watch 5 is a solid update, and I can’t wait to get this thing on my wrist to see if that GPS tech truly lives up to the hype!

Pre-order the Pixel Watch 5 at Best buy

Xremove ads
Pre-order the Pixel Watch 5 at Best buy

Early testing from expert sports watch reviewer DC Rainmaker—who flew to the dense urban canyons of New York City specifically to test this claim—seems to back this up, noting that Google’s GPS accuracy improvements are “incredibly impressive.” If they can pull off this level of accuracy in a standard, everyday smartwatch rather than a bulky “Ultra” model, this could be a huge win for Google, honestly.

Gemini Intelligence and hardware upgrades

And all of this new tracking and AI processing is driven by a few notable hardware improvements under the hood. The Pixel Watch 5 is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, packing 50% more RAM and a 12% CPU boost over the previous generation, making it 20% faster overall.

That extra headroom is largely dedicated to Gemini. Google has introduced “Gemini Intelligence Proactive Suggestions,” which turns complex, multi-step tasks into seamless one-tap actions on your wrist. If someone asks you when a family dinner is, Gemini can automatically pull the info from your calendar and surface it without you having to dig through your phone. You can even interact with it using new double-pinch gestures, and the popular “Raise to Talk” feature now processes core actions instantly with low latency, even when offline.

Xremove ads

Google says the 41mm model will net you up to 30 hours of battery life, while the larger 45mm model can push up to 40 hours with the always-on display.

New Health Guardian features look very interesting

On the health front, Google is also introducing “Health Guardian” features designed to catch subtle shifts in your wellness before they become emergencies. A notable addition is breathing emergency detection. By monitoring your blood oxygen saturation using a combination of sensors and on-device AI, the watch can detect severe drops caused by things like choking or severe pneumonia, and automatically call emergency services if you are unresponsive (launching first in Europe).

The Pixel Watch 5 will also start generating monthly trend summaries for things like blood pressure, sleep breathing quality, and insulin resistance based on your sensor data. For anyone trying to keep a closer eye on their metabolic and cardiovascular health, getting a readable summary directly from your wrist is incredibly practical. It is worth noting that most of these particular features are app-based and will be coming to other Pixel watches later this fall.

Xremove ads

Lastly, it’s worth pointing out that these new features do come with a slight price bump. The Pixel Watch 5 is available for pre-order right now and will hit shelves on August 20. The 41mm model starts at $399, while the 45mm model comes in at $429. There is also a slick $579 Stephen Curry Special Edition in the 45mm size that features an exclusive sweat-wicking performance loop band, arriving a bit later on September 3.

Yes, this is the year of refinement for Google, but overall, I think the Pixel Watch 5 is a solid update, and I can’t wait to get this thing on my wrist to see if that GPS tech truly lives up to the hype!

item.itunes:title: ChromeOS 151 rolls out with new features and security updates
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

Google has officially begun rolling out ChromeOS 151 (version 16733.48.0 / Browser version 151.0.7922.141) to Chromebooks and ChromeOS Flex devices on the Stable channel. While milestone 151 is a modest visual refresh on the surface, the official release notes show off a handful of under-the-hood stability improvements, crucial enterprise policy transitions, and a massive list of 18 security patches.

New Tab page auto-hiding bookmark bar

If you like to keep your workspace minimal and distraction-free, ChromeOS 151 introduces a welcome quality-of-life tweak for the browser’s top bar.

Xremove ads
  • Smart Auto-Hide: Under Settings > Appearance, you will now find explicit controls for bookmark bar visibility. If Chrome detects that you don’t interact with the bookmark bar regularly on the New Tab page, it can automatically tuck it away to maximize vertical screen real estate.
  • One-Click Restore: Whenever the bar is hidden due to low usage, a subtle notification appears allowing you to restore it permanently with a single click.
  • Admin Controls: Enterprise and education administrators can enforce persistent visibility across fleets using the updated BookmarkBarEnabled policy.

Enhanced Safe Browsing for Gemini in Chrome

As Google continues to weave Gemini deeper into the Chrome browser experience, keeping AI-assisted browsing safe against zero-day threats is a top priority.

  • Real-Time Phishing Protection: In ChromeOS 151, Google has integrated real-time Safe Browsing protections directly into active Gemini sessions in Chrome.
  • Zero-Day URL Verification: When using Gemini to summarize web pages, parse research papers, or automate web tasks, Chrome now triggers live Safe Browsing checks to protect users against newly generated malicious domains and deceptive redirect chains.

Legacy Chrome Apps officially cut off in Kiosk mode

As we previously highlighted in our ChromeOS 150 coverage, Google laid out a strict sunset roadmap for legacy packaged Chrome Apps. With ChromeOS 151, the other shoe has officially dropped for Kiosk deployments.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads
  • Kiosk Sessions Cut Off: Legacy Chrome Apps no longer launch in Kiosk mode. Organizations that manage digital signage, interactive displays, or student testing kiosks must migrate their workflows to Progressive Web Apps (PWAs).
  • Managed Guest & User Sessions: If your organization still relies on force-installed Chrome Apps within standard user sessions or Managed Guest Sessions (MGS), those will continue to work for now as part of Google’s phased transition.

ChromeOS Flex legacy GPU update freeze

For those running ChromeOS Flex on older converted PC and Mac hardware, ChromeOS 151 introduces strict hardware compatibility cutoffs to prevent graphical glitches and system freezes.

  • Blocked Hardware: Devices equipped with legacy graphics processors like Intel and AMD GPUs from 2010 and older, and Nvidia GPUs from 2014 and older will no longer receive updates starting with milestone 151.
  • Device Status: Affected machines will remain supported on ChromeOS 150 but will be pinned to that version moving forward.

Stricter Incognito URL filtering & enterprise policies

For school IT administrators and enterprise fleet managers, ChromeOS 151 tightens how administrative rules apply across private windows.

  • Strict Incognito Blocklists: The URLBlocklist policy is now strictly enforced across Incognito sessions, closing previous loopholes where allowlist configurations could accidentally override restrictions in private tabs.
  • Cleaner Wildcard Reporting: Wildcard entries (*) in URLAllowlist policies are now handled more accurately in internal reporting tools, ensuring status logs reflect targeted permissions rather than blanket approvals.

18 high-priority security fixes

ChromeOS 151 is one of the most security-heavy platform updates we have seen in recent cycles. According to the Google Chrome Releases Stable Channel announcement and Chrome Enterprise Release Notes, Google has resolved 18 CVE-tracked vulnerabilities across core system subsystems:

Xremove ads
  • Mojo & Window Management: Fixed a critical integer overflow in Mojo (CVE-2026-13281) and a use-after-free vulnerability in the Aura window manager (CVE-2026-15905).
  • DOM & WebGL: Resolved use-after-free flaws in DOM (CVE-2026-9126), DOM data validation (CVE-2026-15123), and improper implementation in WebGL (CVE-2026-15127).
  • File System & Input: Addressed insufficient policy enforcement in the File System Access API (CVE-2026-12460) and an input handling use-after-free flaw (CVE-2026-15118).
  • Credentials & Web Authentication: Patched password data validation bugs (CVE-2026-12446) and Web Authentication use-after-free flaws (CVE-2026-19166).
  • Payments, Resources & Extensions: Closed use-after-free flaws in Payments (CVE-2026-19155, CVE-2026-19175), Resources (CVE-2026-19141), and untrusted input validation issues in Extensions (CVE-2026-12456) and Web Workers (CVE-2026-19153).

How to get ChromeOS 151 now

ChromeOS 151 is rolling out starting today. To check if the update is ready for your Chromebook:

  1. Open your device Settings.
  2. Select About ChromeOS in the bottom left menu.
  3. Click Check for updates.

From what we can tell over at cros.tech, most currently-supported devices are getting the update right away. Curiously, the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 is left out for the time being. While we’re unsure what the holdup is for that particular device, I’m sure it will be sorted out soon.

item.title: Google Sheets gets big upgrades for Excel file imports and Connected Sheets
item.itunes:title: Google Sheets gets big upgrades for Excel file imports and Connected Sheets
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

Google is rolling out a double-header update for Google Sheets, focusing on two areas where power users often hit friction: converting spreadsheets from Microsoft Excel and analyzing massive datasets in Connected Sheets.

Whether you frequently import .xlsx files from colleagues or query BigQuery databases directly inside a spreadsheet, these new features eliminate manual work and make data presentation significantly cleaner.

Xremove ads

Seamless Excel imports – native tables and live pivot tables

Converting Microsoft Excel files into Google Sheets used to require a fair bit of cleanup. Previously, Excel tables didn’t convert into native Sheets tables, stripping away structural formatting and converting any linked pivot tables into static, uneditable grids. With the latest update to file importing in Google Sheets:

  • Excel tables convert to Sheets tables: Imported Excel tables now automatically map to native Sheets tables, preserving your original formatting, sort controls, and structural benefits right out of the gate.
  • Linked pivot tables remain dynamic: Pivot tables in Excel that rely on table ranges now import as fully functional, interactive pivot tables rather than flat, static data snapshots.

These import improvements mean imported spreadsheets are ready to use immediately without needing to manually rebuild data structures. Table imports are available now, while linked pivot table support is rolling out gradually to all Workspace domains and personal Google accounts.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

Connected Sheets upgrades – list parameters and column aliasing

For organizations using BigQuery, Google is also introducing two key usability features to Connected Sheets designed to make database analysis far more accessible to non-technical team members:

  • List Parameters: When writing BigQuery queries, users can now reference an entire range of cells as a single list parameter. This allows power users or data admins to set up user-friendly input sheets with drop-down menus or selection grids. Collaborators can filter massive database queries dynamically without ever touching the underlying SQL code.
  • Column Aliasing: Database column headers can often be cryptically named or difficult for broader audiences to read. Users can now create presentation-ready column aliases directly within Connected Sheets without changing the underlying database references or breaking existing formulas.

Both Connected Sheets features are rolling out now for all Google Workspace customers and personal account users with Connected Sheets access.

item.title: Pixel 11 lineup’s ultra-incremental upgrades clear the stage for an incredible Googlebook launch
item.itunes:title: Pixel 11 lineup’s ultra-incremental upgrades clear the stage for an incredible Googlebook launch
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

For the past few years in August, those of us that follow tech updates tune in to the Made By Google showcase hoping for solid upgrades in Tensor processing power, GPU, and NPU and hopefully some interesting outer hardware updates to go along with them.

But for this year’s event, initial hands-on reports from publications like 9to5Google and creators like MKBHD and Mrwhosetheboss tell a remarkably consistent story: Google’s 2026 Pixel hardware lineup is a masterclass in incremental, safe iteration. Across all the hardware, you’d be hard-pressed to quickly see a difference in the Pixel 11 lineup versus the Pixel 10. And the same goes for the Pixel Watch 5.

Xremove ads

Across the board, hardware changes are incredibly subtle, prices are up across the line, and the biggest updates are almost entirely driven by AI software tricks. So, to cut right to it, here is a quick, concise rundown of what is being announced, followed by why this relatively tame hardware cycle is actually pretty awesome news for the imminent launch of Googlebook.

The Pixel Portfolio specs & updates at a glance

Pixel 11 ($899)

  • Camera: Upgraded 48MP main sensor (56% more light sensitivity) taking it from a smaller sensor up to standard flagship size, paired with existing ultrawide and 5x telephoto lenses.
  • Charging & Build: Slightly thinner camera bar that sits flush when cased; faster 25W Qi2.2 magnetic wireless charging.
  • Internals & Price: Tensor G6 processor, 12GB RAM, and a doubled 256GB base storage spec. The entry price rises by $100 to $899 (discontinuing the $799 128GB baseline).

Pixel 11 Pro & 11 Pro XL ($1,099 / $1,299)

  • Design & “HiLight”: Replaces the old rear temperature sensor with a circular RGB LED “HiLight” ring around the flash. At launch, it only pulses for Gemini status or specific incoming contact calls.
  • Displays & Cameras: Brighter Super Actua displays (peaking at 3,600 nits); upgraded 50MP main sensor and 48MP telephoto (30% larger sensor for improved 5x portraits).
  • The RAM Caveat: Base 256GB models drop from 16GB of RAM down to 12GB of RAM (you must upgrade to 512GB or 1TB models to get 16GB), while prices jump $100 across both sizes.
  • Faster charging: Upgraded to 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging and faster wired charging for around 75% charge in just 30 minutes.

Pixel 11 Pro Fold ($1,899)

  • Chassis & Durability: 1mm thinner and nearly 10% lighter, swapping out traditional back glass for a new matte polymer/glass fiber composite designed to resist cracking.
  • Screens & Cameras: Brighter 3,600-nit inner/outer displays with slightly slimmer inner bezels; upgraded 48MP main camera and 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.
  • Price: Price increases by $100 to $1,899 for the 256GB/16GB RAM spec.

Pixel Watch 5 ($399 – $429) & Pixel Tag ($29)

  • Pixel Watch 5: Identical external design, but upgraded internally with a Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip, 3GB RAM, 64GB storage, and a new Gemini At a Glance feature and AI-generated watch faces.
  • Pixel Tag: A $29 pill-shaped UWB Bluetooth tracker utilizing Android’s Find Hub network (shipping in November).

Clearing the stage for Googlebook

If you were hoping for substantial hardware upgrades on the Pixel side of things, this year’s Made By Google event might feel a tad bland. But looking at the broader Google ecosystem, this tame refresh creates a fascinating setup for what we all know is coming next.

Xremove ads

Don’t get me wrong: I’m not saying Google planned a muted phone cycle on purpose for the debut of Googlebook, but if Google had unveiled revolutionary phone hardware, wild new foldable designs (like the Z Fold 8), or radical Tensor G6 upgrades, it easily could have sucked all the oxygen out of the room for what we hope is next month’s Googlebook launch. Instead, Google has left the spotlight looking for a new place to shine.

With Googlebook likely to make its official debut in the next 4-6 weeks, Google’s brand-new desktop platform stands to be the most ambitious, innovative hardware and software story Google showcases in 2026 year.

With hardware that looks incredible, software that will bring together the best of desktop, mobile, and AI, and a wide variety of sizes and form factors on the near horizon, there’s no denying the intrigue of Googlebook at this point. The stage is officially set, the spotlight is on, and we couldn’t be more excited for Googlebook season to officially begin!

item.title: Why I’m going to swap some of my third-party trackers for the new Google Pixel Tag
item.itunes:title: Why I’m going to swap some of my third-party trackers for the new Google Pixel Tag
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

After more than two years of refining the Find Hub network, Google has finally decided it is time to make its own tracker. The company just unveiled the Google Pixel Tag, its first-party device tracker, launching on November 11 for $29 (or $99 for a four-pack).

And these tags are a welcome addition for any Android user out there who has struggled to find a solid tracker. If you recall, the launch of the Find Hub (originally Find My Device) network was a bit rocky, so like many of you, I decided to save myself the headache and went with a few Tile Trackers. After one of those finally bit the dust, I decided to give the Find Hub a try and picked up a Pebblebee wallet tracker and tag.

Xremove ads

But after looking at the spec sheet for this new Pixel Tag, it looks like Google has packed in enough solid upgrades that I am ready to pick up a four-pack when they become available. Here is why this little tag has piqued my interest.

True precision with UWB and Channel Sounding

The biggest frustration I’ve had with my current Pebblebee setup is the lack of true precision finding. Because third-party tags generally lack Ultra-Wideband (UWB) chips, you have to rely entirely on audio beeps and vague signal-strength circles on your phone screen to find something stuffed under a couch cushion.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

The Pixel Tag completely fixes this. It combines UWB with a new technology called Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding. If you have a compatible phone (like a Pixel 6 Pro or newer, or the upcoming Pixel 11 series), the Find Hub app will now display exact directional arrows and precise distance measurements down to the inch. If you drop your keys in the house, your phone will physically point you right to them.

Two-way tracking

The other feature that sold me is the two-way tracking button. The Pixel Tag features a physical button that you can press to ring your connected phone. This is a feature that I love on my Pixel Watch, and having that same capability on my keyring or inside my wallet is a nice touch.

On the hardware front, Google went with a sleek, pill-shaped stainless steel design in a grayish color they are calling “Fog.” It is IP67 water and dust resistant, weighs just 12 grams, and uses a standard, user-replaceable CR2032 coin battery that is rated to last over a year. The only minor downside is that, much like an AirTag, there is no built-in hole for a keyring, so you will need to buy a separate accessory to clip it to your bags or keys.

Xremove ads
Check out Today’s Best Chomebook Deals

Deep ecosystem integration

Because this is a first-party Google device, the ecosystem integration is fantastic. It supports Fast Pair for instant setup, allows you to share the tag’s location with up to 10 other people (perfect for shared car keys or luggage), and includes proactive “Left Behind” alerts.

You aren’t just limited to your phone, either. You can locate and ring the tag right from your Pixel Watch, or even ask Gemini through your Pixel Buds to ring the tag for you hands-free.

Finding a spot in my everyday carry

I will point out, though, that I am going to keep my Pebblebee wallet tracker for now, simply because I carry a very slim wallet. But depending on the size of what you carry, the Pixel Tag’s relatively thin 5.4mm design means it could easily slip into some wallets without creating too much bulk. Maybe down the road Google will introduce a dedicated wallet tracker, but as someone who has a tendency to misplace my wallet, I have to stick with my current wallet setup.

Xremove ads

But the beauty of this ecosystem is that since the Pebblebee is already built for the Find Hub, all my trackers will still show up together in the exact same app. For now, I am planning on swapping out the Pebblebee tag in my everyday backpack with the new Pixel Tag to take advantage of that UWB precision, and I am genuinely excited to find some other applications for the other three that come in the four-pack.

At $29, Google is pricing this perfectly in line with the competition while offering significantly better tracking tech for the Android ecosystem. It’s a solid pitch, honestly, and it feels like the complete hardware package Android users have been waiting for. I will definitely be picking up a four-pack when they hit the Google Store in November!

After more than two years of refining the Find Hub network, Google has finally decided it is time to make its own tracker. The company just unveiled the Google Pixel Tag, its first-party device tracker, launching on November 11 for $29 (or $99 for a four-pack).

And these tags are a welcome addition for any Android user out there who has struggled to find a solid tracker. If you recall, the launch of the Find Hub (originally Find My Device) network was a bit rocky, so like many of you, I decided to save myself the headache and went with a few Tile Trackers. After one of those finally bit the dust, I decided to give the Find Hub a try and picked up a Pebblebee wallet tracker and tag.

Xremove ads

But after looking at the spec sheet for this new Pixel Tag, it looks like Google has packed in enough solid upgrades that I am ready to pick up a four-pack when they become available. Here is why this little tag has piqued my interest.

True precision with UWB and Channel Sounding

The biggest frustration I’ve had with my current Pebblebee setup is the lack of true precision finding. Because third-party tags generally lack Ultra-Wideband (UWB) chips, you have to rely entirely on audio beeps and vague signal-strength circles on your phone screen to find something stuffed under a couch cushion.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

The Pixel Tag completely fixes this. It combines UWB with a new technology called Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding. If you have a compatible phone (like a Pixel 6 Pro or newer, or the upcoming Pixel 11 series), the Find Hub app will now display exact directional arrows and precise distance measurements down to the inch. If you drop your keys in the house, your phone will physically point you right to them.

Two-way tracking

The other feature that sold me is the two-way tracking button. The Pixel Tag features a physical button that you can press to ring your connected phone. This is a feature that I love on my Pixel Watch, and having that same capability on my keyring or inside my wallet is a nice touch.

On the hardware front, Google went with a sleek, pill-shaped stainless steel design in a grayish color they are calling “Fog.” It is IP67 water and dust resistant, weighs just 12 grams, and uses a standard, user-replaceable CR2032 coin battery that is rated to last over a year. The only minor downside is that, much like an AirTag, there is no built-in hole for a keyring, so you will need to buy a separate accessory to clip it to your bags or keys.

Xremove ads
Check out Today’s Best Chomebook Deals

Deep ecosystem integration

Because this is a first-party Google device, the ecosystem integration is fantastic. It supports Fast Pair for instant setup, allows you to share the tag’s location with up to 10 other people (perfect for shared car keys or luggage), and includes proactive “Left Behind” alerts.

You aren’t just limited to your phone, either. You can locate and ring the tag right from your Pixel Watch, or even ask Gemini through your Pixel Buds to ring the tag for you hands-free.

Finding a spot in my everyday carry

I will point out, though, that I am going to keep my Pebblebee wallet tracker for now, simply because I carry a very slim wallet. But depending on the size of what you carry, the Pixel Tag’s relatively thin 5.4mm design means it could easily slip into some wallets without creating too much bulk. Maybe down the road Google will introduce a dedicated wallet tracker, but as someone who has a tendency to misplace my wallet, I have to stick with my current wallet setup.

Xremove ads

But the beauty of this ecosystem is that since the Pebblebee is already built for the Find Hub, all my trackers will still show up together in the exact same app. For now, I am planning on swapping out the Pebblebee tag in my everyday backpack with the new Pixel Tag to take advantage of that UWB precision, and I am genuinely excited to find some other applications for the other three that come in the four-pack.

At $29, Google is pricing this perfectly in line with the competition while offering significantly better tracking tech for the Android ecosystem. It’s a solid pitch, honestly, and it feels like the complete hardware package Android users have been waiting for. I will definitely be picking up a four-pack when they hit the Google Store in November!

item.itunes:summary:

As we continue our coverage of the upcoming Googlebook lineup ahead of Google’s expected fall launch event, the puzzle pieces for another major hardware partner have officially locked into place. Joining devices like Dell’s Googlebook XPS 13 ‘Mica’ and Lenovo’s ‘Duet m’ detachable, HP is preparing its own flagship contender for the initial wave of devices running the still-unnamed Aluminium OS.

Originally spotted a year ago in the Chromium Gerrit under the internal development codename ‘Quartz’, recent Geekbench runs, Bluetooth SIG certifications, and accidental listings on HP’s own official Canada portal have confirmed the retail identity of this device: the HP Googlebook 14c.

Xremove ads

The ‘Bluey’ Baseboard & Early Gerrit Finds

In the Chromium Gerrit, ‘Quartz’ was identified as one of the primary derivative boards built on Qualcomm’s “Bluey” baseboard family (alongside Dell’s ‘Mica’ and the ‘Quenbi’ reference design). Early code commits established that ‘Quartz’ was engineered strictly around Qualcomm’s high-end Snapdragon X Elite platform.

Geekbench Benchmark Discovery

In May and June, benchmark entries for an “HP Googlebook 14 inch” surfaced on Geekbench. The software thumbprints confirmed a 12-core Qualcomm architecture with 4 cores running up to 3.42 GHz and 8 cores at 4.01 GHz – a clock layout that aligns perfectly with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite (X1E-80-100) processor.

Xremove ads

The benchmark also confirmed 32GB of RAM and an active Android 17 desktop build. On Geekbench 6, it posted single-core scores around 1,896 and multi-core scores of 9,272, comfortably outperforming mid-range x86 chips like Intel’s Core Ultra 5 115U.

HP Official Site Listing

Confirmation of the “14c” model designation arrived when GbookHub discovered two distinct retail SKUs published on an official HP Canada warranty purchase page:

  • HP Googlebook 14c-cf0010ca
  • HP Googlebook 14c-cf0000ca

Following HP’s traditional Chromebook numbering scheme, cf0000 likely represents the base retail SKU while cf0010 marks a higher-tier memory or storage option.

Xremove ads

Bluetooth SIG Certification

Most recently, a regulatory entry filed by HP Inc. appeared in the Bluetooth SIG database under the product name “HP 14 inch Aluminium Premium Book” and Regulatory Model Number TPN-H111. Historically, HP assigns the TPN-H prefix specifically to Qualcomm Snapdragon-powered hardware (such as the HP Chromebook x2 11 and HP OmniPad 12), further solidifying the connection.

HP Googlebook 14c Key Hardware Specs

Based on the combined certification filings and backend data, here is how the spec sheet for the HP Googlebook 14c is shaping up:

  • Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite (X1E-80-100)
  • CPU Core Layout: 12-core architecture (4x 3.42 GHz + 8x 4.01 GHz)
  • NPU Execution: 45 TOPS Hexagon NPU for local, on-device AI tasks
  • Memory & Storage: Up to 32GB LPDDR5X RAM with solid-state storage options
  • Display: 14.0-inch panel (16:10 aspect ratio)
  • Wireless: Bluetooth 5.4, Wi-Fi 7 capabilities under regulatory designation TPN-H111

Just like we’re seeing with every other Googlebook on the near horizon, this HP Googlebook 14c looks like it will be an absolute beast. I can’t think of any hardware launch I’ve ever seen with such a coordinated, high-end blast of devices all at once; and it all makes me incredibly excited to see what all of these new Googlebook feel like to use in hopefully just a few weeks from now.

item.title: Acer’s new Chromebook 315 is wildly affordable and points to the real future of Chromebooks
item.itunes:title: Acer’s new Chromebook 315 is wildly affordable and points to the real future of Chromebooks
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

We tend to talk a lot about the top end of the market around here. Between the looming arrival of Googlebook and the likely sunset of high-end Chromebook Plus hardware in the consumer space, it is easy to wonder just what the future of Chromebooks will be outside of the EDU and enterprise sectors moving forward.

While Googlebook will soon claim the high-end space for itself on store shelves this fall, devices like the newly refreshed Acer Chromebook 315 represent what I feel like will become the true backbone of ChromeOS in the consumer space over the course of the next year or so.

Xremove ads

Acer’s latest 15.6-inch budget workstation just landed on store shelves, and right out of the gate, both configurations are getting solid launch discounts. More importantly, this laptop is a perfect example of why entry-level Chromebooks aren’t going anywhere anytime soon, and are likely to get better and better over the next few years.

Two budget-friendly configurations on sale

Acer refreshed the 315 line with two distinct models designed for home, student, and family productivity, both featuring a spacious 15.6-inch Full HD (1920 × 1080) display, full numeric keypads, Wi-Fi 6E, and lightweight chassis designs.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

Powered by the MediaTek Kompanio 540 in both a 64GB and 128GB model, the efficient ARM architecture and 4GB of memory is built for all-day battery life and basic web tasks. Normally priced higher, it is currently marked down to $199.00 or $239.00 at Best Buy.

Buy the Acer Chromebook 315 at Best Buy

Why sub-$400 Chromebooks will thrive in the Googlebook era

As we’ve discussed previously, the shift toward Googlebook means the traditional Chromebook Plus category around $700 is probably about to enter a transition phase. High-end hardware partners are gearing up to push premium hardware, Snapdragon X Elite silicon, and Panther Lake SoCs into Googlebook territory.

However, that transition leaves a massive, ripe market wide open: the sub-$400 budget space. For the average consumer who simply needs a large, reliable laptop to check email, pay bills, handle school assignments, stream 1080p video, and manage family schedules, spending $700+ on a laptop is unnecessary. That’s where the still lightweight ChromeOS shines, and where it will continue to dominate for years to come.

Xremove ads

As laptop components become increasingly commoditized and cheaper to manufacture, entry-level hardware should only continue to improve over time:

  • Better Panels for Less: Years ago, a sub-$200 laptop meant suffering through terrible 768p TN panels with awful viewing angles. Today, the Acer 315 gives you a clean 15.6-inch 1080p IPS canvas for two hundred bucks.
  • More Efficient Silicon: Entry-level processors like MediaTek’s Kompanio chips or Intel’s N-series efficiently run lightweight cloud workflows without producing heat or draining tons of battery life.
  • Long-Term Support: With Google guaranteeing up to 10 years of automatic software and security updates, even a $199 purchase offers a decade of functional utility.

Getting maximum value out of a strict budget

Googlebook may represent the future of Google’s ambitious, AI-driven desktop ecosystem, but traditional Chromebooks like the Acer 315 are the reason ChromeOS captured millions of users in the first place.

Buy the Acer Chromebook 315 at Best Buy

By delivering clean, fast, and secure web experiences at prices that fit almost any budget, devices like the Acer 315 prove that you don’t need to spend a fortune to get a solid laptop. If you or a student in your home need a big-screen daily driver without breaking the bank, both new Acer 315 configurations are well worth a look while these launch sales are live.

item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:

Tracking unreleased hardware behind the scenes is always a fun game of connecting development code names to real-world products. For months, we’ve been keeping a close eye on ‘Sapphire’ – a 13-inch MediaTek-powered detachable tablet that stands out as the only tablet-style form factor currently in active development for Google’s upcoming Googlebook ecosystem.

Now, thanks to a fresh listing in the Bluetooth SIG database, we officially have the retail name for this long-awaited detachable: The Lenovo Googlebook Duet m. For anyone who has followed ChromeOS hardware over the last five years, that name should immediately ring a bell.

Xremove ads

Keeping the Duet legacy alive in the Googlebook era

When Lenovo released the original Chromebook Duet back in 2020, it redefined what a budget-friendly 2-in-1 could be. Since then, the Duet moniker has been Lenovo’s go-to branding for lightweight, kickstand-equipped detachables in the Chromebook space.

Seeing Lenovo carry the Duet name over into the Googlebook era while simply appending the “m” designation (which aligns with its MediaTek silicon under the hood) is a fantastic nod to continuity that connects Chromebook legacy to the new Googlebook era.

item.title: Why Google Will Almost Certainly Host a Dedicated Event for the Googlebook Launch
item.itunes:title: Why Google Will Almost Certainly Host a Dedicated Event for the Googlebook Launch
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

Having covered Chromebook, Chromebook Plus and Google hardware announcements for over a decade, I’ve watched plenty of speculation swirl as major launch windows approach. With Google’s August 12 Made by Google event coming up this week and IFA Berlin opening in early September, I’ve seen a lot of folks guessing that the upcoming Googlebook platform will get tagged onto one of those stages.

But if you look at Google’s historical track record with laptop releases, I am convinced those theories miss the mark. Google isn’t going to slip a platform change this massive into a side note: they are almost certainly going to host a dedicated showcase event for the Googlebook debut.

Xremove ads

Made by Google Is for First-Party Hardware Only

The most common theory I’ve heard is that Google will officially launch Googlebook during the August 12 keynote. But anyone who has followed the Made by Google brand since its inception knows that stage is strictly reserved for Google’s in-house hardware like Pixel phones, the Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Buds, and the new Pixel Tag.

Googlebook is a multi-OEM platform manufactured by partners including Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. Because Google isn’t launching a first-party laptop (like Pixel book) for this initial wave, crowding third-party hardware into a Pixel-centric keynote simply doesn’t fit the Made by Google format.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

IFA Berlin isn’t the place for a Googlebook launch

The second popular theory is that Google will use IFA Berlin in September for the rollout. While trade shows are great for OEMs to announce one-off hardware and standard updates, a generic multi-brand trade show is the wrong venue for a fundamental shift the size of Googlebook.

This isn’t just a new laptop line; it is a complete pivot from ChromeOS to an Android-native desktop operating system powered by Gemini Intelligence. Trying to explain screen reasoning, Magic Pointer, and deep Android app integration amidst the noise of a massive trade show would dilute the message and feel completely out of place.

The dedicated showcase strategy

If you want to know how Google will handle Googlebook, look at how they’ve handled major ecosystem upgrades in the past.

Xremove ads

When Google unveiled Chromebook Plus to the world, they didn’t tack it onto a phone event or squeeze it into a trade show. They hosted a dedicated, standalone press event in New York City, bringing in leadership, engineering teams, and OEM partners to give the platform the spotlight it deserved. We saw the exact same dedicated approach for major hardware milestones like the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 launch.

When a release is big enough, Google tends to gather the tech press, they take steps to set up dedicated hands-on demo rooms, and they tend to control the narrative from start to finish. I have to imagine that is what will happen with Googlebook as well.

Google needs dedicated stage time to demonstrate a completely new OS, how all the things we love from ChromeOS have been preserved, why the new hardware is unique and impressive, what big-name apps are available right away, and how Gemini Intelligence will weave through the entire experience.

Xremove ads

What I’m Expecting Next

While the internet will continue to debate whether we’ll see a surprise teaser in August or September, my money is firmly on a standalone Googlebook showcase event this fall. A transition this significant deserves its own stage, its own press briefings, and its own hands-on testing environment. And as soon as official invitations drop, we’ll be here to bring you full hands-on coverage, unboxings, and deep-dive reviews!

item.title: It’s official: Gemini will completely replace the Google Assistant on phones next month
item.itunes:title: It’s official: Gemini will completely replace the Google Assistant on phones next month
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Support our independent tech coverage. Chrome Unboxed is written by real people, for real people—not search algorithms. Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here.
START FREE TRIAL (MONTHLY)START FREE TRIAL (ANNUAL)

The Google Assistant has been slowly replaced by Gemini across all services, but the official end is now near. Google is now sending out emails to users confirming that Google Assistant on mobile devices is being discontinued, with the mandatory transition to Gemini kicking off on September 4, 2026.

Once this update hits your phone over the coming weeks, that’s it. You will no longer be able to use—or switch back to—the legacy Google Assistant on your Android phone, tablet, or paired accessories.

Xremove ads

The final deadline

If you follow our coverage, you might remember that Google originally wanted this transition wrapped up by the end of 2025. They eventually tapped the brakes, pushing the timeline into 2026 to ensure a “seamless transition.” I’m sure that moving everyone from the Assistant to an entirely new LLM-based assistant has been a massive technical hurdle. It sounds like they needed some extra time to iron out the kinks and get Gemini to handle simple, localized tasks with the same speed as the old Assistant.

Check out Today’s Best Chomebook Deals

Now, they are finally confident that Gemini is ready for prime time. When you trigger your assistant after September 4—either by saying “Hey Google” or long-pressing the power button—Gemini will take over.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

It is important to note that this change cascades down to your connected accessories as well. If your phone makes the switch, your paired Wear OS watch, compatible earbuds, and connected Android Auto will also lose legacy Google Assistant access. Interestingly, if you drive a vehicle with Google built-in (Android Automotive), Google Assistant will survive there past the September deadline, at least for now.

The end of an era

Having tested and written about the Google Assistant for many years, I’m feeling a little nostalgic about this one. Don’t get me wrong, the old Google Assistant certainly was not perfect, and we’ve all gotten frustrated a time or two by the “Sorry, I didn’t catch that” response.

But it was the first real digital assistant that was actually helpful in my daily workflow. I still remember quietly whispering to my phone to turn off the lamp in my son’s nursery as I put him to bed for the first time.

Xremove ads

And when I spent countless hours renovating a house a few years ago, installing smart bulbs and smart plugs throughout the rooms was my final touch. Being able to just walk out the front door and tell my phone to turn off the entire house felt like living in the future at the time.

Gemini is pretty incredible and undeniably the future of where Google is taking its hardware, but the classic Google Assistant paved the way for this moment, and it will always have a place in my heart. While I’m happy to see Gemini step up to bat, I think we have to give the Assistant some credit and recognize that this is the end of an era.

A few days ago, I wrote a post about my initial hesitancy with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. After waiting months for it to arrive, my first 24 hours were filled with unexpected friction: my thumb kept blocking the shorter outer screen when scrolling feeds, the inner display felt weirdly oriented for web browsing, and my muscle memory fought the phone’s wider passport aspect ratio at every turn. I even caught myself looking at return options on T-Mobile’s site within 24 hours.

Fast forward a few days and a few small habit tweaks, and I can officially report that saner heads prevailed and I have fallen completely in love with this phone.

Xremove ads

And as it turns out, I’m far from the only one. Reports indicate that due to overwhelming demand, Samsung has ordered an additional 1 million Galaxy Z Fold 8 units to be produced. For an expensive, niche (or not?) foldable, adding a million extra units to the production line right after launch is wild, and it proves that Samsung’s gamble on this new form factor has captured the interest of the phone-buying market.

Buy the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 at Best Buy

Small habit tweaks, big payoffs

Once I stopped fighting the phone and adjusted the way I approached it (I came from the Z Fold 5 and its crazy-thin outer display for 2.5 years, after all), all the benefits of this design really started clicking into place.

Featured Videos

Xremove ads

The outer cover display that felt squat and awkward for about 24 hours has turned into a fantastic screen for quick, one-handed tasks. I can knock out replies, check notifications, or skim headlines without even opening the phone, and the extra width makes typing on the cover screen far more accurate for me than on older, narrower foldables.

When I do open it up, having what amounts to a mini tablet in my pocket at all times has continued to be an incredibly important way that I use my phone throughout the day, with some real added benefits over older, square foldables like the Z Fold 5. Here’s a quick look at how the Z Fold 8 is excelling in tons of ways for me so far:

  • Reading & Content: Reading e-books on the wider inner screen is incredible. and that same orientation is fantastic for browsing the mobile web as well.
  • Media & Gaming: Firing up games or watching videos feels expansive, giving you that full small-tablet canvas without the weird cropping or massive black bars you get with square internal screens.
  • Performance: Powered by top-tier silicon, the phone doesn’t skip a beat no matter what I throw at it.
  • Battery Life: Even with a bit of new phone syndrome making me pick it up and open it constantly throughout the day, I’m comfortably ending heavy-usage days with around 50% battery remaining. That has not been the case with prior foldables for me.

A reminder that good hardware is worth the adjustment

We are creatures of habit. When a new device forces me to change how I hold a phone, scroll a feed, or position my fingers, the immediate reaction is often resistance. But as I’ve learned over the past week, a brief adjustment period is a small price to pay when the hardware on the other side of that curve is this good.

Xremove ads
Buy the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 at Best Buy

Samsung taking a risk on a wider, passport-style foldable seems to have paid off already. If you’ve been on the fence about the Z Fold 8 because of the shape change, take it from someone who almost sent it back: give your brain a day or two to adjust, and you won’t want to go back to a standard slab phone ever again.

item.title: Acer Googlebook 14 leaks confirm Intel Panther Lake, OLED, and more
item.itunes:title: Acer Googlebook 14 leaks confirm Intel Panther Lake, OLED, and more
item.itunes:author: Chrome Unboxed[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:

Following the leak of Dell’s XPS 13 Googlebook, the 2.2-pound ASUS Googlebook, and the Lenovo’s multi-Googlebook lineup, another major launch partner’s flagship has come into focus. As one of the foundational hardware partners of the Chromebook era over the past 15 years, Acer is preparing its own top-tier contender for Google’s upcoming desktop platform.

Uncovered through a combination of Chromium code commits, regulatory filings, and early European retailer database listings, the device long codenamed ‘Moonstone’ has been officially tied to a retail model called the Acer Googlebook 14 (GP714-91N).

Xremove ads

For anyone who has followed Acer’s premium lineup over the years, that model number carries some serious weight. It confirms that Acer is bringing its most successful high-end Windows laptop DNA directly into the Googlebook era. Let’s explore that a bit.

Connecting ‘Moonstone’ to the Acer Googlebook 14

We’ve tracked this device in the Chromium Gerrit for a while, but the more recent finds about the model numbers and leaked retailer info comes via GBookHub. While we don’t have some of the more-juicy images for this particular Googlebook at the moment, we do have quite a few fantastic specs to report:

Featured Videos

Xremove ads
  • The ‘Fatcat’ Reference Board: In the Chromium Gerrit, ‘Moonstone’ is built on Intel’s top-tier ‘Fatcat’ baseboard architecture – the same reference platform powering ASUS’s upcoming ‘Lapis’ Googlebook CX9406. This baseboard was engineered specifically around Intel’s next-generation Panther Lake (Core Ultra) architecture.
  • Model Number Lineage: The GP714 designation is a direct evolution of Acer’s flagship Spin 714 and Chromebook Plus 714 series (historically prefixed as CP714 for “Chromebook Plus” or CBE794 for “Chromebook”). The new “GP” prefix could stand for something like “Googlebook Performance”.
  • Retailer & Certification Filings: The final confirmation came when inventory staging portals across European retail channels and regulatory EEC/FCC filings populated placeholder listings for the GP714-91N SKU, complete with spec breakdowns and expected availability windows.

Hardware specs include Intel Panther Lake and 14-inch OLED

Acer’s 714 series has always been a standout for balanced productivity, quality of build, and high-level specs; and ‘Moonstone’ appears to build on that legacy with cutting-edge hardware across the board:

  • Processor: Intel Core Ultra Panther Lake architecture (featuring Core Ultra 5 325 and Core Ultra 7 355 SKUs).
  • NPU & AI Processing: Integrated neural processing units delivering 47+ TOPS of local execution, specifically tuned for real-time Gemini screen reasoning and multimodal side-panel workflows.
  • Display: 14.0-inch 16:10 OLED panel (offering up to 2.8K / WQXGA+ resolution with 100% DCI-P3 color coverage).
  • Memory & Storage: 16GB or 32GB LPDDR5X RAM paired with high-speed 256GB or 512GB PCIe NVMe SSDs.
  • Googlebook Platform Standards: Dedicated physical Gemini key on the bottom row, top-lid Glow Bar indicator, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, Titan C2 hardware security, and a physical camera privacy shutter.

Why Acer’s 714-series heritage matters for Googlebook

Over the past several years, Acer’s 714 family (from the early, beloved Spin 713 to the latest Chromebook Plus Spin 714 models) has consistently been one of our most frequently recommended laptops for work and daily productivity. They earned that reputation by combining practical port selection, rigid aluminum construction, and excellent display options.

Seeing Acer transition the 714 lineage over to the Googlebook 14 continues to confirm to us that Google’s OEM partners aren’t experimenting with second-tier hardware for this rollout. They are putting their most proven, flagship-level designs behind Google’s latest laptop effort, and it is going to make for an impressive launch.

Xremove ads

With Intel’s superior internal and external hardware, Acer joins the growing list of upcoming Googlebooks that will define the early days of this new laptop segment. With native Android app support eliminating the container overhead of past generations, epic hardware options, and a truly hybrid OS that can handle productivity and entertainment for users, the momentum is only growing for Googlebook ahead of launch. September is going to be awesome!
